# Introduction

## Project Goals
Data breaches represent a major source of financial risk for firms and insurance providers. From an actuarial perspective, modelling the severity of these incidents is essential to quantifying cyber risk and assessing potential insured losses. However, estimating their financial severity is particularly challenging because most organizations do not publicly disclose the financial losses associated with these data breaches. 
Our project focusses on the VERIS Community Database (VCDB), which is one of the largest public sources on breaches. It contains information on 10596 publicly reported incidents and 2683 variables describing their characteristics. Among these data breaches, only around 337 (approximately 3.2%) include a reported monetary loss.  This raises an important statistical issue because the incidents for which financial losses are available may not be representative of all the reported breaches.
The main objective of our project is to investigate which characteristics of data breaches are associated with monetary losses disclosure and to understand how this limited financial information affects the estimation of loss severity. As a secondary objective, we aim to explore whether reported monetary losses can be predicted using statistical methods, while taking into account the limitations of the dataset.

## Research Questions
- Question 1: How do data breach characteristics and monetary loss disclosure rates vary across industry sectors, breach methods and time?
- Question 2: Which incident characteristics are associated with loss disclosure and to what extent can the disclosure event be predicted?
- Question 3: How does reported financial losses vary across industry sectors, and to what extend can their severity be predicted using the available data?
- Question 4: How does the limited availability of financial loss information affect the reliability of loss severity estimates?

## Academic Citations Recommended

Your Related Work section can have **more value when including academic papers (further evidence)** from peer-reviewed journals or conference proceedings, not just books or course materials. Use Google Scholar, university library databases, or specialized actuarial journals to find relevant papers.

**Recommended sources:**

- Academic journals (Insurance: Mathematics and Economics, ASTIN Bulletin, Journal of Risk and Insurance)
- Conference papers (actuarial conferences, data science symposiums)
- Working papers from researchers in your field

**Citation example**: "@azizi2022realestate investigated multi-modal approaches to real estate rental price prediction, demonstrating that models combining tabular data with visual information (property images and satellite imagery) outperform traditional methods relying solely on structured features. Their supervised learning framework fused dedicated neural network branches for each data type, achieving superior performance on 11,105 Swiss rental listings." *(This reference is already in your `references.bib` file and can be cited as `@azizi2022realestate`)*
:::

::: {.callout-note}
## Citing Sources

Always cite your sources properly! In Quarto, use `@citation_key` syntax. The bibliography will be automatically generated from the `references.bib` file.

**Example**: `@azizi2025dsas` renders as: @azizi2025dsas

Add entries to `references.bib` in [BibTeX](https://www.bibtex.com/g/bibtex-format/) format for all sources you cite (every article normally generates BibTeX, otherwise search an online tool that does it).
:::

::: {.callout-warning}
## Avoiding Plagiarism

Make sure to cite all sources that informed your work, including:

- Datasets (with URLs)
- Methods or techniques from papers or tutorials
- Code snippets adapted from online resources
- Inspiration from existing analyses

When in doubt, cite it!
:::

::: {.callout-caution}
## Common Mistake

Don't just list your research questions without context. Explain **why** each question matters and **how** it relates to your dataset and project goals.
:::
